chapter_theme: Asking is permitted, even graceful, when the giver is one who can't conceal. The chapter then goes further and says that the world needs askers, since without them giving, fame and even being alive would lose their point. It closes by telling the asker not to be angry at refusal.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar opens by limiting the chapter: this is begging without disgrace, allowed only when poverty brings one to the edge of death (1051-1052). Then the nature of those worth asking (1053-1057), why the world needs askers (1058-1059), and what the asker must be like (1060). The following chapter, on dread of begging, argues nearly the reverse.

1051.reading: Ask if you find those worth asking; if they withhold, the blame is theirs and not yours.
1051.nuance: The chapter starts by moving the moral burden from the asker to the withholder. Parimelazhagar says such givers understand before anything is said, and the blame sticks to them as a stain does on pure white cloth, because they're rare.

1052.reading: Even asking is pleasure to a person, if what is asked for comes without suffering.

positions.position: The suffering is the asker's: the courting, reading the giver's moods and being refused, which is spared if the giver anticipates.
The suffering is that of both, giver and receiver.

1053.reading: Even standing and asking before those of unconcealing heart who know கடன் has a certain beauty.
1053.nuance: முன்நின்று is significant: for Parimelazhagar merely standing is enough, and it's the absence of spoken words that keeps the grace.

positions.position: கடன் is honour, and it is the asker's: he reads 963 to explain why such a giver can sense a poor person's dignity.
கடன் is social obligation, the duty of helping.
கடன் is the giver's sense of duty.

1054.reading: Even asking is like giving, from those who don't conceive of concealment even in a dream.
1054.nuance: An extraordinary equivalence that erases the difference in rank. Parimelazhagar tempers it: asking brings no fame, but nor does it damage any you already have, so that is all the likeness. The strong statement is the verse's and the caveat is his.

1055.reading: It's because there are people on earth who don't conceal that askers take up standing before them.
1055.nuance: Parimelazhagar adds the alternative: without such people they would give up their lives, since they can't give up honour. So the existence of generous people is what keeps them alive.

1056.reading: If one sees those without the affliction of concealment, every affliction of poverty is destroyed at once.
1056.nuance: Concealing is called இடும்பை, the same word as poverty, so the verse treats the wealthy miser as a sufferer too. The cure comes merely at the sight (காணின்). Manakkudavar concludes one shouldn't ask from those who are merely rich.

1057.reading: If one sees those who give without scorn and contempt, the heart is delighted and rejoices deep inside.
1057.nuance: The joy lies in being given to without being lowered. உள்ளுள் உவப்பது goes deeper than the material relief, and it's the manner of the gift that's being measured.

1058.reading: If there were no askers, this wide cool world would be wooden puppets coming and going.

positions.position: Without someone to give to, others would earn no fame or merit, and they might as well be lifeless.
positions.quote: அவர்க்கு ஈதலைச் செய்து புகழும் புண்ணியமும் எய்தாமையின், உயிருடையரல்லார்

positions.position: Asking and giving are the order of the world, so asking shouldn't be treated as low.
positions.quote: இரத்தலும் ஈதலும் உலகியல்பாதலான், இரத்தல் இழிவென்று கொள்ளப்படா

positions.position: He changes the subject: those who won't let askers near are the puppets.

1059.reading: What renown could givers have, if there were none who want to ask and take?
1059.nuance: The logic has an uncomfortable side: if givers' renown requires askers, a world without poverty would be poorer in virtue. The verse doesn't address this, and it treats askers as a need, not as a problem.

1060.reading: The one who asks shouldn't be angry; the affliction of his own poverty is proof enough.
1060.nuance: His poverty proves that wealth is hard to come by, so the refuser may have a real reason. This turns the sufferer's own case into a reason for patience. It is a counterweight to 1051, which puts blame on those who withhold.

links.note: Consecutive chapters open in direct opposition. 1051: ask if you find those worth asking. 1061: not asking, even of those who give gladly and are as dear as eyes, is ten million times better. Parimelazhagar's solution makes 1051 apply only at the edge of death; the verses themselves don't state this.

The wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை) marks a lack of real life in both. In 1020 it's a person without shame, and in 1058 a world without askers. Each chapter finds what makes movement into life, one in an inner quality and one in a social transaction.

232 says that all that speakers praise rests on those who give to askers. 1059 makes the dependence explicit: the fame needs the asker as well. The asker turns out to be necessary for a fame that seemed the giver's alone.

Asking from the right person is like giving (1054), yet asking even water for a cow is the most degrading thing the tongue can do (1066). The chapters give opposite values to one act, and the difference of giver doesn't fully explain it, since 1061 refuses even the best givers.
Parimelazhagar himself cites 963 here: the poor must stand tall, and asking without speaking lets them do so. The honour chapter's demand shapes how begging can be done at all.

source_issues: 1052, 1059: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
1052: Kalaignar's text ends with stray material, ஊ. தெளிவு உரைத் தெளிவுக்கு.
1054: Parimelazhagar's gloss has சுரத்தலை where கரத்தலை is expected, apparently a transcription error.
1056: Pope's gloss has 'evil of begging' for நிரப்பிடும்பை, where his couplet has 'plague of poverty'.
1060: Pope's couplet ('from wrath must stand aloof') is loose; the Tamil is simply that the asker should not be angry.
